name: Colin Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a paint-can lid press and test the first seam after each die change. I came from council grounds work, so I am still a junior learning press settings at fifty-eight with secondary schooling. Weekend premiums give me higher-than-usual operator pay, and I like seeing a tight lid leave the line.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and how do you use new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Rina works at a hardware shop, and our grown children live in their own homes. We have a housing loan, about nine months saved and plenty of other metal plants nearby. I have never used AI tools; I follow the paper setup sheet and ask the senior operator before a new setting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the lid crew that the AI talk can settle down. A paint-can lid still needs a proper seam test before anybody stacks a pallet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I came into the metal plant from council grounds work and am still a junior on the lid press at fifty-eight. Weekend premiums lift my wage above the usual rate, Rina works at a hardware shop, and we have nine months saved with our grown children living separately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the weekend press shifts and test the first lid after each die change. From each full paid month I would put a fresh amount against our housing loan, and I would keep using the paper setup sheet the senior operator gave me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel calm about the factory. I know the press has more to teach me, but the household can cover a repair without borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check on a lid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I press it onto a sample can and look for a loose curl at the rim. The senior operator checks my first changeover before we release a batch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you used AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, never. I finished secondary school and learn a machine by standing beside someone who already runs it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask management what the new software does to orders before it brings a robot stacker into our press area. The crew should see a guarded demonstration and a written rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A camera could check simple curls while a stacker takes the pallet job. I am still junior on the press, so one of my weekend shifts could go first; Rina’s hardware-shop pay alone would not cover our housing loan and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my present shifts and ask for the next two rosters. If the plant offers paid supervised practice behind a tested guard, I would consider learning the stacker after an experienced operator proves it; after an actual hours cut I would apply only for posted reachable press jobs whose net pay after travel covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about my own hours. I do not mind a useful machine, but I mind a roster that shrinks before anyone explains why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start training now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI tools and would not start with a video. I would need an actual paid safe place with a qualified operator and a stopped press.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you find another plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are several nearby, but I would check a real posting, weekend rate and travel cost. A larger headline wage does not always leave more money at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the press crew that thinking AGI may arrive by 2028 when I am sixty, while capable lid-handling robots come around 2031 when I am sixty-three. Office planning changes first, then physical press work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most junior press hours to disappear when robots can set dies and stack lids. Nine months saved buys a search, but Rina’s shop wage cannot replace my weekend pay indefinitely; I would lie awake over the housing loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cancel the planned car replacement and ask for written staffing dates. If my shifts end, I would apply for posted reachable metal work only where net pay after travel covers our bills; if no adequate role appears, I would ask the lender about temporary terms before a missed payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed by a large expected wage loss. I can visit nearby shops, but I cannot make them hire me in the same week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need actual pension and household figures that cover the loan, food and repairs. Nine months saved does not tell me what the next ten years pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own homes and bills. I would ask for a lift to an interview if one is free, not a regular loan payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AGI in 2031 finds me sixty-three and capable press robots around 2034 find me sixty-six. Five years is long enough for the plant to offer a proper paid maintenance place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the first lid test but I am still learning the die settings. A maintenance qualification could help if another nearby metal shop posts a job, but I would not spend our reserve on an unfunded course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the press shift and add fresh full-month wages to savings after bills. If the plant offers me a funded die-maintenance course on paid time with a qualified fitter and stopped-press practice, and a posted reachable job pays our bills after travel, I would enrol; after qualifying, I would apply for that role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious but able to compare the terms. A real fitter beside a stopped press is worth more to me than a screen full of promises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would safe practice involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fitter would isolate the press and let me measure a worn die before replacing it. I would need an offered paid slot and a checked guard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no maintenance job is posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid press shift and check local operator postings if hours fall. I would not buy a certificate for a job that exists only in a meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AGI in 2036 finds me sixty-eight and capable press robots around 2039 find me seventy-one. Ten years is time to check retirement income and keep paid work safe for anyone who needs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rina and I hope to stop full-time shifts before seventy-one, but I cannot say what the housing loan or pension will look like then. Our grown children have their own bills; they are not a retirement account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the lid press running and save fresh full-month surplus after the housing payment. I would request pension and loan figures with Rina; in the first year after 2036, if still employed because we need wages, I would compare actual rosters and apply after sustained cuts only for posted reachable safe work with bill-covering net pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about distant robots while our current pay and reserve are sound. The figures will decide when I stop, not the date on a poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if verified pension and Rina’s confirmed pay cover housing, food and repairs. I would keep safe paid work if that sum falls short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn new controls then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask a qualified person for an offered paid safe lesson if I still had the job. I cannot promise the plant will have a press place for me thirteen years from now.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable press robots around 2031 could take junior shifts before our housing loan is cleared. Written staffing dates, funded paid safe training and posted reachable work at bill-covering net pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who will test the first lid after a robot changes the die. A sample can still has to seal before a family opens it.

headlineQuote: A sample can still has to seal before a family opens it.
portrait: **Colin**, 58, is a junior lid-press operator after a late move from grounds work, with secondary schooling and developing machine skill.
His **hardware-shop partner**, grown children, housing loan, higher weekend pay, nine-month reserve and many nearby plants give options.
He has **never used AI**, prefers paper settings and would accept only offered funded paid safe mechanical training.
Fast robots threaten **junior press hours** at sixty-three; longer warning supports conditional die training and verified retirement planning.
biggestWorry: **Fast physical robots** could remove junior press shifts around 2031 before his household can afford to stop work.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, offered funded safe training and posted reachable work at bill-covering net pay would help.
